chapterTitle: Everything Loss for Christ — Pressing On Toward the Prize, Citizens of Heaven
themeTitle: “I Count All Things to Be a Loss for the Excellency of Knowing Him”

scripture.text: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you, to me indeed is not tiresome, but for you it is safe.
scripture.understanding: Τὸ λοιπόν — “finally,” or “as for the rest” — and Paul still has two chapters to go; it marks a transition, not an ending. “Rejoice in the Lord.” The command is not just to rejoice, but to rejoice ἐν κυρίῳ, in the Lord — joy anchored in a Person. Then Paul says that writing the same things again is not ὀκνηρός — tiresome, a bother — for him, and for them it is ἀσφαλής, safe, a safeguard. Repetition of the basics is not boring; it is protection.

scripture.text: Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the false circumcision.
scripture.understanding: Three sharp warnings, each beginning with βλέπετε — watch out for, keep your eyes on. “The dogs” — Jews used κύνες, dogs, as a word for unclean Gentiles; Paul turns it back on teachers who insisted Gentiles be circumcised. “The evil workers” — ἐργάται κακοί, people who boasted of their works of the law but whose work was destructive. And the κατατομή — the mutilation. Paul makes a pun: not περιτομή (circumcision) but κατατομή, cutting to pieces. Circumcision demanded as a requirement for salvation is mere mutilation of the flesh.

scripture.text: For we are the circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh;
scripture.understanding: “For we are the circumcision” — the true people of God — defined by three marks: we λατρεύω, worship, serve as priests, πνεύματι θεοῦ, by the Spirit of God; we καυχάομαι, boast, in Christ Jesus; and we have no πεποίθησις, confidence, in the σάρξ — the flesh, meaning all human performance, pedigree and religious achievement. The true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29).

scripture.text: though I myself might have confidence even in the flesh. If any other man thinks that he has confidence in the flesh, I yet more:
scripture.understanding: Paul could compete on their terms and win. If anyone thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, Paul has more. He is about to list his credentials — not to boast, but to show that he gave them up knowing exactly what they were worth.

scripture.text: circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; concerning the law, a Pharisee;
scripture.understanding: Seven credentials, four inherited and three achieved. Περιτομῇ ὀκταήμερος — circumcised on the eighth day, as the law required, not as an adult convert. Of the γένος, the race, of Ἰσραήλ. Of the tribe of Βενιαμίν — the tribe that gave Israel its first king, Saul, whose name Paul bore, and that stayed loyal to Judah. A Ἑβραῖος ἐξ Ἑβραίων — a Hebrew of Hebrews, Hebrew-speaking parents, nothing diluted. As to the law, a Φαρισαῖος — a member of the strictest party (Acts 26:5).

scripture.text: concerning zeal, persecuting the assembly; concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless.
scripture.understanding: As to ζῆλος — zeal — a persecutor of the church. That is what zeal for the law had led him to: hunting down Christians. As to the righteousness that is in the law, γενόμενος ἄμεμπτος — found blameless. By the external standard of law-keeping, no one could fault him. Paul is not saying he was sinless; he is saying he was impeccable by the measure his opponents used.

scripture.text: However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.
scripture.understanding: The great reversal, in the language of accounting. Whatever was κέρδος — gain, profit, the column of assets — these he has ἡγέομαι — counted, reckoned (perfect tense: a settled verdict) — as ζημία, loss, damage, a write-off, διὰ τὸν Χριστόν, because of Christ. He moved them from one side of the ledger to the other.

scripture.text: Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ
scripture.understanding: And he goes further: not just those things, but πάντα, all things, he counts as loss διὰ τὸ ὑπερέχον — because of the surpassing worth — of knowing Christ Jesus “my Lord.” Notice the personal pronoun: my Lord. For Him Paul has ζημιόω — suffered the loss of — all things, and he counts them σκύβαλα. Σκύβαλον was a coarse word for refuse — dung, or scraps thrown to the dogs. Paul uses the strongest word available. Compared to Christ, his finest achievements were rubbish.

scripture.text: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith;
scripture.understanding: “And be found in him” — at the judgment, when God looks, Paul wants to be found inside Christ. Not having μὴ ἔχων ἐμὴν δικαιοσύνην — a righteousness of my own, from the law — but the righteousness that is διὰ πίστεως Χριστοῦ, through faith in Christ, “the righteousness which is from God by faith.” Two kinds of righteousness: one manufactured by human effort, one received as a gift from God. This verse is Romans and Galatians compressed into one sentence.

scripture.text: that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, becoming conformed to his death;
scripture.understanding: The purpose of it all: τοῦ γνῶναι αὐτόν — that I may know Him. Not know about Him; know Him personally, experientially. Then three parts of that knowing: the δύναμις, power, of His resurrection; the κοινωνία, sharing, of His παθήματα, sufferings; and συμμορφιζόμενος — being conformed, shaped together with — His death. Power and suffering are not opposites in the Christian life. They are two sides of knowing the same Christ.

scripture.text: if by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead.
scripture.understanding: “If by any means I may καταντάω — arrive at — the ἐξανάστασις — the out-resurrection — from the dead.” A rare, intensified word, found only here in the New Testament: resurrection out from among the dead. Paul's “if by any means” is not doubt about his salvation (he has just said he is found in Christ). It expresses the humility and eagerness of someone straining toward a goal he has not yet reached.

scripture.text: Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus.
scripture.understanding: Paul guards against any idea that he has arrived. Not that I have already ἔλαβον — received it — or am already τετελείωμαι — made complete, perfected. Possibly a correction to people who claimed spiritual perfection. But διώκω — I pursue, I chase, the word Paul once used for persecuting the church — so that I may καταλαμβάνω, seize hold of, that for which Christ Jesus seized hold of me. Christ caught Paul on the Damascus road; now Paul runs to catch what Christ caught him for.

scripture.text: Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do. Forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before,
scripture.understanding: “Brothers” — a tender address. Paul does not λογίζομαι, reckon, himself to have laid hold of it yet. “But one thing” — ἓν δέ. A single-minded life. Τὰ μὲν ὀπίσω ἐπιλανθανόμενος — forgetting what lies behind: his past achievements, his past failures, the church he persecuted. Τοῖς δὲ ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτεινόμενος — stretching out toward what lies ahead; a runner's body straining forward, leaning toward the finish line.

scripture.text: I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
scripture.understanding: Κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω — I pursue toward the σκοπός, the mark, the finish post a runner keeps his eyes on — for the βραβεῖον, the prize — τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ θεοῦ, of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus. At the games, the victor was called up to the official's stand to receive his prize. Paul is running toward the moment God calls him up.

scripture.text: Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, think this way. If in anything you think otherwise, God will also reveal that to you.
scripture.understanding: “As many as are τέλειοι — mature, perfect — think this way.” A deliberate twist on verse 12: Paul is not perfected, but mature people are those who know they are not and keep pressing on. Maturity is the awareness that you have not arrived. And if anyone thinks differently on some point, God will ἀποκαλύπτω — reveal — that to them. Paul trusts God to correct His people.

scripture.text: Nevertheless, to the extent that we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule. Let us be of the same mind.
scripture.understanding: Whatever point we have φθάνω — reached, attained — let us στοιχέω, keep in step, march in line, by the same standard. Στοιχέω was used of soldiers keeping rank. Live up to what you already have.

scripture.text: Brothers, be imitators together of me, and note those who walk this way, even as you have us for an example.
scripture.understanding: “Brothers, be συμμιμηταί of me” — join together in imitating me. And σκοπέω — keep your eye on, the word of 2:4 — those who walk according to the τύπος, the pattern, you have in us. Christianity is learned by watching living examples.

scripture.text: For many walk, of whom I told you often, and now tell you even weeping, as the enemies of the cross of Christ,
scripture.understanding: “For many walk… as the ἐχθροί — enemies — of the cross of Christ.” And Paul says this κλαίων, weeping, sobbing aloud. He does not denounce them with satisfaction. He grieves over them. Who are they? Probably professing believers whose lives contradicted the cross — people who lived for their appetites. Paul had warned the Philippians often.

scripture.text: whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who think about earthly things.
scripture.understanding: Four marks. Their τέλος, end, is ἀπώλεια — destruction. Their god is the κοιλία — the belly, appetite, physical desire of every kind. Their δόξα, glory, is in their αἰσχύνη, shame — they boast in what they should be ashamed of. And they φρονέω, set their minds, on τὰ ἐπίγεια — earthly things. The mind of Christ (2:5) versus the mind set on earth.

scripture.text: For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ;
scripture.understanding: “For our πολίτευμα — citizenship, commonwealth — is in heaven.” To proud Roman citizens in a colony of Rome, this was a powerful image. Philippi was Rome in miniature, far from Rome, under Roman law, waiting for imperial visits. The church is a colony of heaven on earth. And from heaven ἀπεκδεχόμεθα — we eagerly await — a σωτήρ, Saviour. In Philippi, the title “saviour” was given to the emperor. Paul gives it to Jesus.

scripture.text: who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.
scripture.understanding: When He comes, He will μετασχηματίζω — transform, change the outward form of — τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν, the body of our lowliness, our humble state, to be σύμμορφον — conformed, sharing the same form — to τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, the body of His glory. The same word as 3:10: conformed. And He will do it κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν — by the working, the energy — by which He is able to ὑποτάσσω, subject, all things to Himself. The power that will put the universe under His feet will remake your body.

visualMeditations.title: Two Columns in the Ledger
visualMeditations.image: Picture an accountant's ledger, the kind a Roman merchant kept, with two columns: profit on one side, loss on the other. In the profit column, written in the careful hand of a young Pharisee, are the most impressive religious credentials in Israel: circumcised on the eighth day; of the people of Israel; of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; a Pharisee; zealous enough to persecute the church; blameless in law-keeping. Now picture a man in chains taking a pen and drawing a line through every entry — and rewriting them, one by one, in the loss column. Then he writes underneath, in large letters, a single word that would make a polite reader wince: σκύβαλα. Garbage. Dung. Scraps for the dogs.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul did not give up worthless things. He gave up the best things he had — the very things every devout Jew of his day would have envied. And he gave them up not reluctantly but gladly, because he had found something of “surpassing worth”: knowing Christ Jesus his Lord. Jesus told a parable about a man who found treasure hidden in a field, and “in his joy, he goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field” (Matthew 13:44). Paul is that man. The question for you is not whether you have bad things to give up. It is whether you are trusting good things — your upbringing, your religious record, your achievements, your moral reputation — for your standing with God. Those must go into the loss column too.

visualMeditations.title: The Runner Leaning at the Line
visualMeditations.image: Picture the final stretch of a race in the stadium. The crowd is roaring. A runner, chest heaving, legs burning, does not look back over his shoulder to see who is behind him — that would cost him the race. He does not glance at the crowd. His eyes are fixed on the finish post, the σκοπός. And in the final strides his whole body leans forward, neck stretched, arms reaching — the word Paul uses is ἐπεκτείνομαι, stretching out toward something. Beyond the line, on a raised stand, the official waits to call the winner up to receive the prize.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul describes the Christian life in this posture. He has not arrived (v. 12). He is not perfect. But he presses on. “One thing I do. Forgetting the things which are behind” — not only his past achievements, which he has already counted as loss, but also his past failures, including the terrible memory of persecuting the church. Neither the trophies nor the scars are allowed to slow him down. “Stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.” What is behind you that keeps pulling your eyes back — a success you keep living in, or a failure you keep reliving? The race is ahead. Forget it, and lean toward Christ.

visualMeditations.title: A Colony of Heaven
visualMeditations.image: Picture the forum of Philippi on a feast day of the emperor. Hundreds of miles from Rome, the city looks like Rome: Latin inscriptions, Roman dress, Roman law, temples to the emperor, veterans proud of their citizenship. Everyone is waiting for news from the capital, and perhaps for an imperial visit. Now picture a small group of believers meeting in Lydia's house nearby. They too are citizens of a distant capital. They live under its laws, speak its language, wait for its King. But their capital is not on the Tiber. It is in heaven, and their King is not Caesar, whom the city calls saviour. It is Jesus.
visualMeditations.meaning: “For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 20). The Philippians understood colonies. They knew what it meant to belong to a city they did not live in, and to shape their lives by its laws. Paul says the church is exactly that: an outpost of heaven on earth. That changes how you live — your values, your loyalties, your hopes — because you are not ultimately a citizen of this world. And it changes how you see your body. The King is coming, and “who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory” (v. 21). Your weak, aging, struggling body will be made like His resurrection body. The people whose god is their belly are living for the colony. You are living for the capital.

structure.label: Rejoice — and Beware (v. 1-3)
structure.body: Paul tells them again to rejoice in the Lord, then warns sharply against those who demand circumcision; the true circumcision are those who worship by the Spirit, boast in Christ and put no confidence in the flesh.

structure.label: Paul's Credentials (v. 4-6)
structure.body: If anyone could boast in the flesh, Paul could: circumcised on the eighth day, of Israel, of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, a zealous persecutor, blameless in law-righteousness.

structure.label: Everything Loss for Christ (v. 7-11)
structure.body: He counts all these gains as loss — as rubbish — for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ, to be found in Him with the righteousness that comes from God through faith, and to know the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings.

structure.label: Pressing On (v. 12-16)
structure.body: Not yet perfect, Paul presses on, forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, toward the prize of God's upward call; the mature think this way and live up to what they have attained.

structure.label: Two Ways to Walk (v. 17-21)
structure.body: Imitate Paul and those who live like him, not the many who live as enemies of the cross, whose god is their belly and whose minds are on earthly things; our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we await the Saviour who will transform our bodies like His glorious body.

sections.heading: Dogs, Mutilators and the True Circumcision
paragraphs: Chapter 3 opens with the command that runs through the whole letter — “rejoice in the Lord” (v. 1) — and then turns abruptly to a warning so sharp that some scholars have wondered whether it comes from a different letter. It need not; Paul is simply returning, as he says, to things he has told them before, because repetition is a safeguard (v. 1). “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the false circumcision” (v. 2). These are almost certainly Jewish-Christian teachers who insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be fully saved — the same group Paul fought in Galatians. Whether they had reached Philippi yet or were simply a threat, Paul wants the church forewarned.

His language is deliberately provocative. Jews sometimes called Gentiles “dogs,” unclean animals outside the covenant. Paul turns the insult around: those who insist on circumcision as a condition of salvation are the real outsiders. And he makes a pun: they are not the περιτομή, the circumcision, but the κατατομή, the mutilation — cutting the flesh without any spiritual meaning. Then he defines the true people of God: “we are the circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh” (3:3). This echoes Romans: “circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit not in the letter” (Romans 2:29). And Colossians 2:11 says believers have received “a circumcision not made with hands… in the circumcision of Christ.”

The key phrase is “no confidence in the flesh.” In Paul, “flesh” here does not mean the physical body; it means human nature relying on its own resources — ancestry, ritual, performance, moral achievement. The false teachers had confidence in the flesh: in a physical rite and in law-keeping. And Paul says he could beat them at their own game (v. 4). He then lists seven credentials (vv. 5–6). Four he was born with: circumcised on the eighth day, an Israelite, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews. Three he achieved: a Pharisee, a zealous persecutor of the church, and blameless in the righteousness of the law. By the standard his opponents valued, Paul was at the very top. Acts confirms it: he was trained “at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3) and lived “after the strictest sect of our religion… a Pharisee” (Acts 26:5).

sections.heading: Rubbish Compared to Christ: Two Kinds of Righteousness
paragraphs: Then comes one of the most personal and radical passages Paul ever wrote. “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ. Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ” (vv. 7–8). The language is that of a balance sheet: κέρδος (profit) and ζημία (loss). Everything Paul once counted as profit he has moved into the loss column. And then he uses σκύβαλα, a coarse word for dung or scraps thrown to dogs. He is not being polite. Compared to Christ, his finest religious achievements are garbage.

Why? Verse 9 explains: so that he may “be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith.” There are only two kinds of righteousness: one that is “my own,” produced by my law-keeping and effort, and one that is “from God,” received as a gift through faith. They cannot be combined. If you add your own righteousness to Christ's as part of your standing before God, you have not understood the gift. This is the doctrine of Romans and Galatians in a single verse: “being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they didn’t subject themselves to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3).

But Paul's goal is not merely a legal standing. It is a relationship: “that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, becoming conformed to his death” (v. 10). He wants to know Christ personally and experientially. And he puts power and suffering side by side. Many want the power of the resurrection without the fellowship of the sufferings. Paul knows they come together. To know the risen Christ is to share His life, including His sufferings and His way of death — the self-giving of 2:5–8. And the goal is “the resurrection from the dead” (v. 11), using a rare intensified word, ἐξανάστασις, the out-resurrection, rising from among the dead. Justification, relationship, transformation and resurrection: everything Paul wants is found in Christ.

sections.heading: Not Yet Arrived: Pressing On as Citizens of Heaven
paragraphs: Lest anyone think Paul claims to have reached spiritual perfection, he immediately corrects it: “Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus” (v. 12). There is a beautiful play here: Christ “took hold of” Paul on the Damascus road; now Paul presses on to take hold of what Christ took hold of him for. And the verb διώκω, to pursue, is the same word he used in verse 6 for persecuting the church. The energy that once drove him to hunt Christians now drives him toward Christ.

Then the runner's image: “One thing I do. Forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (vv. 13–14). “Forgetting” does not mean erasing memory; Paul has just listed his past in detail. It means refusing to let the past — whether achievements or failures — determine his present course. A runner who looks back loses ground. And then a deliberate paradox in verse 15: “as many as are perfect” (τέλειοι, mature) should think this way. The mature are precisely those who know they have not arrived and keep running. Spiritual maturity is not the sense of having attained; it is the passion to keep pressing on.

Verses 17 to 21 contrast two ways of living. Paul invites them to imitate him and those who walk the same way (v. 17), and warns, with tears, of “many” who “walk… as the enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who think about earthly things” (vv. 18–19). These appear to be people within the Christian orbit whose lives were governed by their appetites — the opposite extreme from the legalists of verse 2. Paul's tears show that his warnings are not cold. And then the great alternative: “our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ; who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory” (vv. 20–21). For a Roman colony whose citizens prized their status and called the emperor “saviour,” the meaning was unmistakable. Believers are a colony of heaven. Their true King, their true Saviour, is coming from the capital, and when He arrives, He will transform their humble bodies into the likeness of His glorious one, by the same power with which He will subject all things to Himself.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: Paul's autobiography in verses 4 to 6 is confirmed by Acts and Galatians. To a crowd in Jerusalem he said: “I am indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God” (Acts 22:3). To King Agrippa: “after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee” (Acts 26:5). And to the Galatians: “beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God, and ravaged it. I advanced in the Jews’ religion beyond many of my own age among my countrymen, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (Galatians 1:13–14). Philippians 3:7–8 is the verdict that man reached after meeting the risen Christ.

The exchange of verse 8 — losing everything to gain Christ — is the response Jesus described in His parables of the kingdom: “the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found, and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field… having found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:44, 46). Notice the joy. Paul does not count all as loss grimly; he does it because he has found something of surpassing worth. And the race of verses 12 to 14 echoes his words to the Corinthians — “Run like that, that you may win” (1 Corinthians 9:24) — and the call of Hebrews: “let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1).

The heavenly citizenship of verse 20 is a theme across the New Testament. Paul tells the Ephesians, “you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). Hebrews says the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13), and “they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them” (Hebrews 11:16). And the promise of the transformed body in verse 21 is echoed by John: “we know that, when he is revealed, we will be like him; for we will see him just as he is. Everyone who has this hope set on him purifies himself, even as he is pure” (1 John 3:2–3). The hope of heaven does not make believers careless about earth. It makes them pure.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “what is thrown to the dogs, i.e. refuse (ordure).” This is the only occurrence of the word in the New Testament, and it was a crude, vulgar term — it could mean excrement, or food scraps tossed out for dogs. Strong's definition is striking given that Paul has just called the false teachers “dogs” in verse 2. Paul deliberately chose the harshest word available to describe how he now views his former religious credentials compared to Christ. Polite translations soften it, but Paul did not. Things that are excellent in themselves — heritage, discipline, moral achievement — become rubbish when they are trusted as a substitute for Christ.

Strong's defines ζημία as “detriment” and κέρδος as “gain.” Both are commercial words, used in ledgers and business dealings. Ζημία is used in Acts 27:10, 21 for the loss of cargo in a shipwreck — goods thrown overboard to save the ship. That is a powerful parallel. Paul's credentials were valuable cargo, but they would have sunk him; he threw them overboard to be saved. Jesus used the related verb: “For what will it profit a man, if he gains the whole world, and forfeits his life?” (Matthew 16:26). In Christ, the accounting is reversed: what looked like gain is loss, and what looked like loss is the only real gain.

Strong's: “to ‘know’ (absolutely) in a great variety of applications and with many implications.” In biblical usage γινώσκω often carries the sense of personal, experiential knowledge — even the intimate knowledge of marriage (Matthew 1:25). When Paul says “that I may know him,” he does not mean information about Christ, which he already had in abundance. He means deeper personal acquaintance: knowing Christ as one knows a friend, by sharing life with Him. Jesus defined eternal life this way: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ” (John 17:3). Christianity is not a set of beliefs about Christ. It is knowing Him.

Strong's: “to stretch (oneself) forward upon.” This is the only occurrence in the New Testament. It combines two prepositions with the verb to stretch: ἐπί (upon, toward) and ἐκ (out), giving the vivid picture of a runner whose whole body is stretched out toward the finish — neck forward, arms reaching, leaning into the tape. It is the opposite of a casual jog. Paul's Christian life is not a leisurely walk but a straining sprint toward Christ. And it requires the first half of the verse: forgetting what is behind. You cannot strain forward while looking back.

Strong's: “a community, i.e. (abstractly) citizenship (figuratively).” This is its only occurrence in the New Testament. In the Greek world πολίτευμα could mean a citizen body, a colony of citizens living abroad, or the government and constitution of a state. In Philippi — a Roman colony whose citizens were proud to be registered as citizens of Rome far from Rome — the word was perfectly chosen. Believers are a colony of heaven on earth: their names are enrolled in heaven (Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3), their laws come from heaven, their loyalty belongs to heaven's King, and they wait for Him to come from there. Paul linked it to the verb in 1:27: live as citizens worthy of the gospel.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: the credentials you are still trusting, the past that keeps pulling your eyes backward, and the city you are really living for.

items.title: What Is Still in Your Gain Column?
items.body: You probably do not trust in circumcision or tribal ancestry. But the Spirit wants to search your ledger. What gives you a quiet sense that God should accept you? Your church upbringing, your years of service, your moral record, your theological knowledge, your giving, your ministry, your discipline? None of these are bad in themselves. But if any of them are in your gain column — counted toward your standing before God — they have become a substitute for Christ. Paul counted his best credentials as rubbish so that he could be found in Christ, with a righteousness that comes from God. Move everything into the loss column. Then you will discover what you actually gain.

items.title: Looking Back Over Your Shoulder
items.body: Something behind you keeps pulling your eyes back. Perhaps it is a past success you keep living in — the season when ministry flourished, the job you were good at, the version of yourself you miss. Or perhaps it is a past failure you keep reliving — the sin, the broken relationship, the thing you did that you cannot forgive yourself for. Paul had both: a brilliant past and the blood of Christians on his hands. He chose to forget both and press on. The Spirit is asking you to let go — not to pretend the past did not happen, but to stop letting it run your race. What do you need to stop looking back at?

items.title: Which City Are You Living For?
items.body: Paul wept over people whose god was their belly and whose minds were set on earthly things. The Spirit is asking you, gently but plainly: what are your thoughts set on most of the time? Your comfort, your appetites, your possessions, your status, your plans for this life? Or the city you belong to and the King who is coming from it? Your citizenship is in heaven. That does not mean ignoring earth; it means living on earth by heaven's laws, with heaven's values, waiting for heaven's King. What is one area of your life where you have been living as a citizen of the colony rather than of the capital?

audit.title: The Ledger Check
audit.body: Draw two columns: Gain and Loss. In the Gain column, write the things you are tempted to rely on for your standing before God or your sense of worth — background, achievements, record, gifts. Then ask: am I trusting any of these instead of Christ? Write verse 9 underneath and cross out anything you have been leaning on.

audit.title: The Rear-View Check
audit.body: Write down one past success and one past failure that you think about often. For each, ask: is this helping me run forward, or pulling my eyes back? What would it mean to “forget” it in Paul's sense — not erase it, but refuse to let it set my course?

audit.title: The Mind Check
audit.body: For one day, notice what your mind keeps returning to when it is free — in the shower, driving, waiting. Write down the main themes at the end of the day. Are they mostly earthly things or the things of the city you belong to? What does that reveal?

practices.title: Counting the Loss
practices.body: Take the list from your Ledger Check. Read verses 7 to 9 aloud. Then, one by one, pray over each item: “Lord, I count this as loss compared to knowing You. I do not trust it. I want to be found in You, with Your righteousness.” If something on the list is a good thing — your family, your work, your gifts — thank God for it as a gift, and then place it below Christ. Finish by praying verse 10 aloud: “That I may know Him.”

practices.title: One Thing
practices.body: Paul's life was organised around “one thing” (v. 13). This week, write at the top of each day: “One thing I do: press on toward Christ.” Then choose one concrete action that day that moves you toward knowing Him better — an extended time in Scripture, a costly act of obedience, a sacrifice, a conversation about Christ, fasting from something that distracts you. At the end of the week, look back at the seven actions and ask what changed in how you see your daily priorities.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, I rejoice in You. Guard me from every teaching that would add to Your finished work, and keep me from putting confidence in the flesh. I confess that I have kept things in my gain column — my background, my record, my achievements, my religious performance — and I have leaned on them for my standing before God. Today I count them all as loss compared to the surpassing worth of knowing You, my Lord. I let go of my own righteousness. I want to be found in You, with the righteousness that comes from God through faith. Lord, I want to know You — the power of Your resurrection and the fellowship of Your sufferings, being conformed to Your death, so that I may attain to the resurrection from the dead. I have not arrived. I am not perfect. But I press on to take hold of that for which You took hold of me. Help me to forget what is behind — my successes and my failures — and to strain forward toward what is ahead, toward the prize of Your upward call. Break my heart, as You broke Paul's, for those who live as enemies of Your cross. Lift my mind from earthly things. I am a citizen of heaven. I am waiting for my Saviour. Come, Lord Jesus, and transform this lowly body to be like Your glorious body. In Your name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Moses Refuses the Treasures of Egypt
storyConnections.summary: Moses was raised in Pharaoh's palace as the son of Pharaoh's daughter, with access to the wealth, education and power of the greatest empire on earth. When he grew up, he went out to his own people and saw their suffering, and he identified with them rather than with the palace. Hebrews says he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to share ill-treatment with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin, because he counted the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he looked to the reward. Moses' ledger and Paul's are the same: the best things the world could offer, moved into the loss column for the surpassing worth of Christ.

storyConnections.title: The Man Who Could Not Let Go
storyConnections.summary: A man ran up to Jesus, knelt before Him and asked what he must do to inherit eternal life. When Jesus listed the commandments, he answered that he had kept them all from his youth — like Paul, blameless by the standard of the law. Jesus looked at him and loved him, and told him that one thing was lacking: he should sell what he had, give to the poor, and come and follow Him. And the man's face fell, and he went away grieving, because he had great possessions. He had the same opportunity Paul had — to count his gain as loss for Christ — and he could not do it. Jesus told His disciples how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom, and then said that what is impossible with men is possible with God. Paul was the proof.

storyConnections.title: Lot's Wife Looks Back
storyConnections.summary: When the angels rescued Lot and his family from Sodom, they told them to flee and not to look back. As fire fell on the city, Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt. Jesus Himself pointed to her as a warning about the day of His coming: remember Lot's wife, and whoever seeks to save his life will lose it. Her heart was still in the city she was leaving; she could not forget what lay behind. Paul's command to forget the things behind and strain toward what is ahead, and his reminder that our citizenship is in heaven, is the opposite of her backward look. A believer whose heart is still in Sodom cannot run toward the heavenly city.
